 Why you need to fix your sleep schedule – and eight tips to help you do it
 Research has indicated that not getting enough sleep can be bad for your heart
 Camilla Foster Monday 02 November 2026 11:35 EST

 New research has shown that an inconsistent bedtime could have a significant and long-term effect on your heart health.
 Researchers working on the National Institutes of Health ’s All of Us research programme conducted an analysis of the sleep data from more than 10,000 adults wearing activity-tracking technology.
 The study revealed that irregular sleep timing from night to night over a period of six months was associated with a 20 to 23 per cent greater risk of significant cardiovascular issues, such as strokes, heart attacks and heart failure.
 At the same time, having more sleep cycles each night was linked with a 28 per cent lower chance of atrial arrhythmia, which is a common irregular heartbeat issue.
 Unusually, the study also linked long sleep cycles to a 55 per cent higher risk of heart attack or stroke.
 open image in gallery Waking up at the same time every day is the first step towards getting a consistent amount of rest ( Alamy/PA ) As mounting proof underscores the significance of getting consistent sleep habits, we spoke to Adele Crow, who is the clinical lead occupational therapist at Cygnet Health Care.
 As an expert, she shared her advice on how to course-correct an erratic sleep schedule.
 1. Wake up at the same time every day
 “Try and stick to a realistic time to wake up every day that works for you,” Crow advised. “We all have an internal body clock, called a circadian rhythm , and if you’re getting up at a regular time each day that will train your internal body clock.
 “When we have that regular sleep pattern, our body knows and will help us to wake up naturally at that time.”
 If you’re not sure about your best sleep schedule, consider starting a sleep diary to spot patterns.
 “Keeping a sleep diary might be able to help you figure out what the best wake-up time is for you, how much sleep your body needs, helps map out how you’re feeling in your mood and concentration, and how many times you’re waking up during the night as well,” the occupational therapist said.
 2. Consider a sunrise alarm clock
 Struggle to get up? A sunrise alarm clock could stop you from hitting snooze.
 “A sunrise alarm clock gradually lights up the room when it’s darker in the autumn and winter and can help you gradually wake up,” Crow said.
 3. Avoid daytime naps
 “During the day we build up what’s called sleep pressure, also known as tiredness. Therefore, if we nap during the day, we reduce that sleep pressure, which then makes it harder for us to fall asleep, or means we are more likely to wake up during the night because we’ve not got that sleep pressure,” Crow explains. “So, try to avoid napping during the day where possible.”
 But if you can’t survive without napping, keeping your naps under 30 minutes was the best way to limit the damage, Crow said.
 “If you do have a nap that’s longer than 30 minutes, then you will go into deep sleep, which then makes it harder for you to fall into deep sleep at night,” Crow said.
 4. Get outside during the day
 “Make sure that you get outside and get some exposure to daylight, especially in the mornings,” Crow advised.
 Daylight is our body’s natural sleep medication and controls our body’s internal body clock, Crow said.
 open image in gallery Spending time outside during the day is important for getting a good night’s rest ( Alamy/PA ) “Going outside and getting some light in the morning initially suppresses melatonin (our body’s sleep hormone) production, but then also helps give us a boost of melatonin in the evening, which is when we need it,” Crow said.
 “In the winter months, it can be harder to get that natural light. But it’s still really important that you get out in the light when you can.”
 5. Move your body in the morning
 “It’s really important that we get moving, especially in the mornings, because aerobic exercise helps our body release chemicals which tells the brain that we’re awake and alert and raises our body temperature,” Crow explains.
 “Exercise also helps increase our sleep pressure as well, which will then help us to sleep at night.”
 open image in gallery Exercising and getting moving in the morning can help the body to wake itself up ( Alamy/PA ) But she advised against exercising too close to bedtime.
 “Try not to exercise too much at night because if our body temperature spikes and the chemicals and hormones are rushing and telling our body that our brain that we’re awake and alert, then it will be harder to get to sleep,” Crow said.
 6. Stay out of bed until bedtime
 “Try not to spend too much time in your bedroom outside of the times that you’re sleeping,” recommends Crow. “You want your brain to associate the room with sleep, rather than a room which you do other things in.”
 7. Adjust your sleeping environment
 “Think about your sleeping environment, such as the sensory factors in your room,” Crow advised. “Avoid clutter and too much visual stimulus.”
 Lighting and comfort could make a big difference.
 “You might want to consider putting some blackout blinds up or changing your duvet. Think about what factors you could adjust to help improve your sleep,” Crow said.
 8. Create a wind-down routine
 “Think about what you’re doing in that 30 minutes before bed to wind down,” Crow advised. “You could dim the lightning in your room, switch off any screens and do some calming activities such as reading a book, listening to music or some journaling – whatever you need to do to tell your brain that you’re ready for bed.”
